source.title: A List of Problems on the Reverse Mathematics of Ramsey Theory on the Rado Graph and on Infinite, Finitely Branching Trees

accepted.question_text: Over RCA0, are the following four principles equivalent: (A) the Halpern-Lauchli Theorem for any finite number of trees; (B) Milliken Ramsey theorem for strong trees on one finitely branching infinite tree with no terminal nodes; (C) the canonical partition theorem for colorings of a fixed finite graph inside the Rado graph; and (D) for every k at least 2, the Rado graph has the rainbow Ramsey property for k-bounded colorings?

evidence.quote: The following implications are known as ZFC, or even just ZF, results: with (A) => (B) => (C) => (D).
(1) Are any of (A) - (D) equivalent over RCA0?

accepted.question_text: Is the reverse-mathematical strength of the rainbow Ramsey theorem for edges in the Rado graph strictly greater than the reverse-mathematical strength of the rainbow Ramsey theorem for pairs of natural numbers?
accepted.context_brief: Edges in Rado graph versus pairs

evidence.quote: (2) Is the rainbow Ramsey theorem for edges in the Rado graph strictly stronger than the rainbow Ramsey theorem for pairs on the natural numbers?

accepted.question_text: Fix any graph G with three vertices and any k at least 2. Over RCA0, assuming the rainbow Ramsey theorem for k-bounded colorings of triples of natural numbers, does it follow that the rainbow Ramsey theorem holds for k-bounded colorings of copies of G inside the Rado graph?

evidence.quote: What about k-bounded colorings of graphs with three vertices in the Rado graph versus k-bounded colorings of triples of natural numbers?
does the rainbow Ramsey theorem for k-bounded colorings of copies of G in the Rado graph follow over RCA0

accepted.question_text: For each d, is the reverse-mathematical strength of the strong-tree version of the Halpern-Lauchli Theorem for d trees strictly weaker than the corresponding strength for d+1 trees?

evidence.quote: (4) Is the reverse math strength of the (strong tree version) Halpern-Läuchli Theorem for d trees strictly weaker than for d + 1-trees?

accepted.question_text: For each d, is the reverse-mathematical strength of the strong-tree version of the Halpern-Lauchli Theorem for d trees strictly stronger than the reverse-mathematical strength of the somewhere dense matrix form for d trees?
accepted.context_brief: Strong-tree versus somewhere dense matrix form

evidence.quote: (5) Is the reverse math strength of the strong tree version of Halpern-Läuchli for d trees strictly stronger than the somewhere dense matrix form for d trees?

accepted.question_text: Does the statement that the Halpern-Lauchli Theorem holds for any finite number of trees have the same reverse-mathematical strength as the statement that Milliken theorem for colorings of finite strong trees holds?

evidence.quote: Does “The Halpern-Läuchli Theorem holds for any finite number of trees” have the same strength as “Milliken’s Theorem for colorings of finite strong trees holds”?

accepted.question_text: Does the reverse-mathematical strength of Milliken theorem depend on the height of the finite trees being colored?

evidence.quote: (7) Does the strength of the Milliken Theorem depend on the height of the finite trees being colored?

accepted.question_text: Does the reverse-mathematical strength of either the Halpern-Lauchli Theorem or Milliken theorem depend on the splitting properties of the trees, such as whether the trees are two-branching, three-branching, or finitely but unboundedly branching?

evidence.quote: Does the strength of either the Halpern-Läuchli Theorem or the Milliken Theorem depend on the splitting properties of the trees?
are two-branching trees weaker than three-branching trees,..., weaker than finitely but unboundedly branching trees?

accepted.question_text: What is the reverse-mathematical strength of statement (D), namely that for every k at least 2 the Rado graph has the rainbow Ramsey property for k-bounded colorings?

evidence.quote: (D) The Rado graph has the rainbow Ramsey property, for k-bounded colorings, for each k >= 2.
(9) What is the Reverse Mathematics strength of the statement (D)?

accepted.question_text: For the Rado graph, does the rainbow Ramsey property for k-bounded colorings have the same reverse-mathematical strength as the rainbow Ramsey property for (k+1)-bounded colorings?

evidence.quote: (10) Does the rainbow Ramsey property for k-bounded colorings of the Rado graph have the same reverse math strength as for (k + 1)-bounded colorings?

accepted.question_text: Does the rainbow Ramsey theorem for the Rado graph have the same reverse-mathematical strength as the canonical partition theorem of Sauer for colorings of a fixed finite graph inside the Rado graph?

evidence.quote: (C) Canonical partition theorem on colorings of a fixed finite graph inside the Rado graph.
(11) Does the rainbow Ramsey theorem for the Rado graph have the same reverse math strength as the canonical partition theorem of Sauer?

accepted.question_text: How do the reverse-mathematical strengths of the rainbow Ramsey theorem for the Rado graph compare when the colorings are of different finite graphs; are the strengths all the same, or does the number of vertices in the finite graph being colored affect the strength?

evidence.quote: How do the strengths of the rainbow Ramsey theorem for the Rado graph compare for colorings of different finite graphs?
Are they all the same, or does the number of vertices in the finite graph being colored affect the strength?
